claim: The dominant models of learning and memory, such as Hebbian plasticity, propose that experiences are transformed into memories through input-specific synaptic plasticity at the time of learning.
source: The dominant models of learning and memory, such as Hebbian plasticity, propose that experiences are transformed into memories through input-specific synaptic plasticity at the time of learning.
evidence: This is a statement about established models in the field, drawing from scientific consensus.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is neither strictly input-specific nor restricted to the time of its induction.
source: However, synaptic plasticity is neither strictly input-specific nor restricted to the time of its induction.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established scientific knowledge about synaptic plasticity properties.

claim: A weak associative conditioning protocol in mice, where optogenetic stimulation of sensory thalamic input to the amygdala was paired with a footshock, produced no detectable memory.
source: First, we established a weak associative conditioning protocol in mice, where optogenetic stimulation of sensory thalamic input to the amygdala was paired with a footshock, but no detectable memory was formed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: When the thalamic input was potentiated minutes before or after the weak conditioning, the associative experience was converted into a lasting memory.
source: However, when the same input was potentiated minutes before or after, or even 24 hr later, the associative experience was converted into a lasting memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: When the thalamic input was potentiated 24 hr after the weak conditioning, the associative experience was converted into a lasting memory.
source: However, when the same input was potentiated minutes before or after, or even 24 hr later, the associative experience was converted into a lasting memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Potentiating an independent input to the amygdala minutes after the pairing produced a lasting memory.
source: Importantly, potentiating an independent input to the amygdala minutes but not 24 hr after the pairing produced a lasting memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Potentiating an independent input to the amygdala 24 hr after the pairing did not produce a lasting memory.
source: Importantly, potentiating an independent input to the amygdala minutes but not 24 hr after the pairing produced a lasting memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The process of transformation of a transient experience into a memory is neither restricted to the time of the experience nor to the synapses triggered by it.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that the process of transformation of a transient experience into a memory is neither restricted to the time of the experience nor to the synapses triggered by it; instead, it can be influenced by past and future events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Experience-dependent synaptic plasticity is widely regarded as the substrate of learning.
source: Experience-dependent synaptic plasticity is widely regarded as the substrate of learning (Kandel et al., 2016; Mayford et al., 2012; Squire and Kandel, 2009), but see, (Gallistel and King, 2009; Gershman, 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: The dominant cellular model of learning, Hebbian plasticity, requires temporal and spatial specificity.
source: The dominant cellular model of learning, Hebbian plasticity, requires temporal and spatial specificity: the strength of a memory can be modified temporally only at the time of learning and spatially only at the encoding synapse and no other (Malenka and Bear, 2004; Maxwell Cowan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on Hebbian plasticity.

claim: The most studied form of Hebbian plasticity is homo-synaptic long-term potentiation (homoLTP) of synaptic transmission.
source: The most studied form of such plasticity is homo-synaptic long-term potentiation (homoLTP) of synaptic transmission or, as commonly known, LTP (Malenka and Bear, 2004; Maxwell Cowan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is neither temporally restricted to the time of the induction of the potentiation nor spatially confined to a single synapse.
source: However, synaptic plasticity is neither temporally restricted to the time of the induction of the potentiation nor it is spatially confined to a single synapse (Harvey and Svoboda, 2007; Koch, 2004; Stuart et al., 2016; Yuste, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: HeteroLTP has been identified in various synaptic pathways where a transient LTP can be stabilized by the induction of a more stable form of LTP on other synaptic inputs.
source: HeteroLTP has been identified in various synaptic pathways where a transient LTP can be stabilized by the induction of a more stable form of LTP on other synaptic inputs (Fonseca, 2013; Frey et al., 2001; Frey and Morris, 1997; Shires et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: HeteroLTP can be induced in non-potentiated synapses as long as they receive subthreshold stimuli.
source: In fact, heteroLTP can be induced in non-potentiated synapses as long as they receive subthreshold stimuli (Harvey et al., 2008; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007; Hedrick et al., 2016; Murakoshi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A temporal window for heteroLTP induction ranges from minutes to tens of minutes.
source: Subsequent studies established a temporal window, ranging from minutes to tens of minutes, within which heteroLTP can be induced (Bear, 1997; Clopath et al., 2008; Govindarajan et al., 2006; Kastellakis et al., 2016; Kastellakis and Poirazi, 2019; O'Donnell and Sejnowski, 2014; Redondo and Morris, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: An LTP protocol can produce synaptic potentiation at the stimulated synapses (Hebbian homoLTP) and also modulates plasticity at other synapses that converge onto the same neuron (non-Hebbian heteroLTP).
source: Thus, an LTP protocol can produce synaptic potentiation at the stimulated synapses (Hebbian homoLTP), but it also modulates plasticity at other synapses that converge onto the same neuron (non-Hebbian heteroLTP).
evidence: This is a synthesis of established knowledge about LTP mechanisms.

claim: Reducing the number of pairings and the duration of the footshock resulted in a less robust conditioned response.
source: Importantly, reducing the number of pairings with shorter US duration resulted in a significant reduction in the CR 24 hr following the conditioning (7%±2) (Figure 1a and b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: High frequency stimulation (HFS) of the thalamic inputs to the lateral amygdala applied 24 hr after a weak thalamic associative conditioning significantly increased the CS-evoked freezing.
source: Left: High frequency stimulation (HFS) of the thalamic inputs (Th) to the lateral amygdala (LA) applied either 24 hr (WTh + 24hHFSTh, corresponding to panel a, top branch), or immediately after a weak thalamic associative conditioning (WTh + HFSTh, corresponding to panel a, middle branch), significantly increased the CS-evoked freezing (n=9; One-way ANOVA, FInteraction (2, 23)=8.202, p-value = 0.0020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: HFS of the thalamic input immediately after a weak associative conditioning significantly increased the CS-evoked freezing.
source: Left: High frequency stimulation (HFS) of the thalamic inputs (Th) to the lateral amygdala (LA) applied either 24 hr (WTh + 24hHFSTh, corresponding to panel a, top branch), or immediately after a weak thalamic associative conditioning (WTh + HFSTh, corresponding to panel a, middle branch), significantly increased the CS-evoked freezing (n=9; One-way ANOVA, FInteraction (2, 23)=8.202, p-value = 0.0020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The optical homoLTP protocol produced potentiation of in vivo field potentials in the lateral amygdala.
source: Brief light pulses at the recording site produced in vivo field potentials which were potentiated by optical homoLTP stimulus (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Most neurons within the lateral amygdala receive direct projections from the cortical regions (auditory/associative).
source: In addition to the thalamic inputs, most neurons within the LA receive direct projections from the cortical regions (auditory/associative) (Choi et al., 2021; Humeau et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Prolonged illumination of axons expressing a red-shifted ChR2 reversibly renders the axons insensitive to further light excitation.
source: A previous study demonstrated that prolonged illumination of axons expressing a red-shifted ChR2 reversibly renders the axons insensitive to further light excitation (Hooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Activation of thalamic axons expressing ChrimsonR by short pulses of blue light was effective in evoking a field potential, but the light failed to produce a discernible response when the illumination coincided with a 500ms yellow light of sub milliwatt intensity.
source: While activation of the thalamic axons expressing ChrimsonR by short pulses of blue light (10–15 mW) was effective in evoking a field potential, the light failed to produce a discernible response when the illumination coincided with a 500ms yellow light of sub milliwatt intensity. This was evident in whole-cell recording from slices (Figure 2a–c) as well as in vivo with single-pulse or high-frequency stimulation (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: With co-illumination, fiber volley and excitatory postsynaptic potential largely disappeared.
source: With the co-illumination, fiber volley, and excitatory postsynaptic potential (the pre- and postsynaptic components, respectively) largely disappeared (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The responses gradually recovered to their original values within hundreds of milliseconds after co-illumination.
source: The responses gradually recovered to their original values within hundreds of milliseconds (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The observed insensitivity of ChrimsonR to blue light is more likely caused by the transient inactivation of the opsin rather than by transmitter depletion or subthreshold depolarization of the axons.
source: These data indicate that the observed insensitivity of ChrimsonR to blue light is more likely caused by the transient inactivation of the opsin rather than by the transmitter depletion or subthreshold depolarization of the axons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The induction of heteroLTP protocol immediately after the weak conditioning produced a long-term conditioned response.
source: Similar to homoLTP, the induction of heteroLTP protocol immediately after the weak conditioning produced a long-term CR (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In mice expressing opsin only in the thalamic inputs, the same manipulation failed to produce a conditioned response.
source: In mice expressing opsin only in the thalamic inputs, the same manipulation failed to produce a CR (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: HeteroLTP protocol delivered 24 hr after weak conditioning failed to produce a significant conditioned response.
source: In this condition, heteroLTP protocol, in contrast to homoLTP protocol, failed to produce a significant CR (Figures 1b and 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1b and 3c.

claim: The thalamic→LA pathway is required for the formation of contextual fear memory.
source: It has been shown that the thalamic→LA pathway, in addition to its role in the auditory-cued fear learning, is required for the formation of contextual fear memory (Barsy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The thalamic inputs convey a footshock signal to the lateral amygdala.
source: The time-locked GCaMP activity of the thalamic projections to the onset of the footshock was evident, demonstrating that the thalamic inputs convey the footshock signal to the LA (Figure 4b), confirming previous findings (Barsy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 4b and citations.

claim: In thalamic-lesioned mice, the footshock-evoked response in the lateral amygdala was significantly reduced.
source: In the thalamic-lesioned mice, the footshock-evoked response in the LA was significantly reduced (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Immediate homoLTP stimulus proved to be effective in producing a lasting conditioned response even for the unpaired conditioning.
source: Immediate homoLTP stimulus, indeed, proved to be effective in producing a lasting CR even for the unpaired conditioning (Figure 4f)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Neither unpaired conditioning alone, nor optical homoLTP stimulus in naïve animals produced a conditioned response.
source: it is noteworthy that neither unpaired conditioning alone, nor optical homoLTP stimulus in naïve animals produced a CR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: HomoLTP protocol when delivered 24 hr after unpaired conditioning produced an increase in freezing, but the value was not statistically significant.
source: HomoLTP protocol when delivered 24 hr later, produced an increase in freezing; however, the value was not statistically significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The heteroLTP protocol produced a conditioned response comparable in magnitude to the paired conditioned animals.
source: In this group, the heteroLTP protocol produced a CR, which was comparable in magnitude to the paired conditioned animals (compare Figure 4h with Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4h and 3c.

claim: Following footshocks, optical LTP delivery on the cortical inputs induced lasting potentiation on the thalamic pathway despite the fact that footshock on its own did not produce any detectable form of postsynaptic potentiation.
source: Indeed, we observed that following footshocks, optical LTP delivery on the cortical inputs induced lasting potentiation on the thalamic pathway despite the fact that footshock on its own did not produce any detectable form of postsynaptic potentiation (Figure 4i and j).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Without a footshock, high-frequency stimulation (HFS) of the cortical inputs did not induce synaptic potentiation on the thalamic pathway.
source: Without a footshock, high-frequency stimulation (HFS) of the cortical inputs did not induce synaptic potentiation on the thalamic pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2d.

claim: Footshock on its own does not produce a detectable synaptic potentiation in thalamic inputs, but it is required for heterosynaptic potentiation of this pathway.
source: Therefore, although footshock on its own does not produce a detectable synaptic potentiation in thalamic inputs, it is required for heterosynaptic potentiation of this pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A left-shifted input-output curve and lasting potentiated field responses were observed in both thalamic and cortical pathways on the recall day.
source: We observed a left-shifted input-output curve as well as lasting potentiated field responses in both thalamic and cortical pathways (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Mice showed significantly increased freezing response during optical stimulation on the recall day.
source: Fifteen minutes later, mice were moved to a new context and tested for their memory recall by activating their thalamic inputs. Mice showed significantly increased freezing response during optical stimulation (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: A weak conditioning protocol that was not followed by an optical LTP protocol on the cortical inputs failed to produce synaptic potentiation of the thalamic inputs.
source: A weak conditioning protocol that was not followed by an optical LTP protocol on the cortical inputs failed to produce synaptic potentiation of the thalamic inputs (tested 2 hr and 24 hr after the LTP protocol; Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: Stimulation of the thalamic inputs with a weak induction protocol resulted in a transient form of potentiation that regressed to the baseline within 90 min.
source: Stimulation of the thalamic inputs with a weak induction protocol (Figure 5d) resulted in a transient form of potentiation that regressed to the baseline within 90 min (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo slice electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: When the weak conditioning protocol was followed by a strong conditioning protocol on the converging cortical inputs, it produced a stable form of potentiation that lasted for the entire duration of the recording.
source: However, when the weak conditioning protocol was followed by a strong conditioning protocol on the converging cortical inputs, it produced a stable form of potentiation that lasted for the entire duration of the recording (Figure 5e and f).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo slice electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5e and f.

claim: The strength of a memory can be enhanced by potentiating the synaptic inputs encoding that memory (homoLTP) prior to or after an aversive conditioning.
source: We found that the strength of a memory can be enhanced by potentiating the synaptic inputs encoding that memory (homoLTP) prior to or after an aversive conditioning.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Potentiation of an independent synaptic input (heteroLTP) minutes after the conditioning is as effective in strengthening the memory.
source: Importantly, we show that potentiation of an independent synaptic input (heteroLTP) minutes after the conditioning is as effective in strengthening the memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In vivo electrophysiology recordings from freely moving animals showed a strong correlation between synaptic potentiation and the successful recall of the aversive memory, as late as 24 hr after the induction of heteroLTP.
source: Our in vivo electrophysiology recordings from freely moving animals showed a strong correlation between synaptic potentiation and the successful recall of the aversive memory, as late as 24 hr after the induction of heteroLTP; all the mice with the successful recall had a successful potentiation of the synaptic input (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology and behavioral data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: The efficacy of heteroLTP stimulus when delivered 24 hr after the conditioning drops considerably, whereas homoLTP retains its capacity to strengthen the memory.
source: The efficacy of heteroLTP stimulus when delivered 24 hr after the conditioning drops considerably, whereas homoLTP retains its capacity to strengthen the memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing homoLTP and heteroLTP at different time points.

claim: These data are consistent with the Synaptic Tagging and Capture (STC) model, which predicts that a heteroLTP protocol can stabilize a transient synaptic potentiation when induced minutes, but not hours prior to or after a weak LTP protocol.
source: These data are consistent with the Synaptic Tagging and Capture (STC) model, which predicts that a heteroLTP protocol can stabilize a transient synaptic potentiation when induced minutes, but not hours prior to or after a weak LTP protocol (Redondo and Morris, 2011; Rogerson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of established models, supported by citations.

claim: HomoLTP as well as heteroLTP effectively uncover an aversive memory in an unpaired conditioning paradigm.
source: Perhaps the most surprising finding in this work is that homoLTP as well as heteroLTP effectively uncover an aversive memory in an unpaired conditioning paradigm; this form of conditioning on its own does not produce a detectable memory (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Unpaired conditioning not only fails to produce a conditioned response, but also does not induce synaptic potentiation, as predicted by Hebbian models of plasticity.
source: It is important to note that previously we have shown that unpaired conditioning not only fails to produce a CR, but also does not induce synaptic potentiation, as predicted by Hebbian models of plasticity (Nabavi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In anesthetized mice that received multiple footshocks, no synaptic potentiation of thalamic inputs was detected.
source: Similarly, in our in vivo recording, where anesthetized mice received multiple footshocks, no synaptic potentiation of thalamic inputs was detected (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: The same protocol, when followed by heteroLTP stimulus, resulted in a synaptic potentiation that lasted for the entire duration of the recording.
source: The same protocol, however, when followed by heteroLTP stimulus, resulted in a synaptic potentiation that lasted for the entire duration of the recording (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: This phenomenon is more in line with the Cross Talk model, which predicts heteroLTP can result in potentiation of synapses that have undergone subthreshold stimulation but no potentiation.
source: In this respect, this phenomenon is more in line with the Cross Talk model, which predicts heteroLTP can result in potentiation of synapses that have undergone subthreshold stimulation but no potentiation (Harvey et al., 2008; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of established models, supported by citations.

claim: The subthreshold activation could be the result of stimulation, and hence priming of the thalamic inputs by footshock.
source: In the present context, the subthreshold activation could be the result of stimulation, and hence priming of the thalamic inputs by footshock.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: In the absence of a footshock, LTP stimulus produces neither a conditioned response nor a heterosynaptic potentiation.
source: This is supported by the fact that in the absence of a footshock, LTP stimulus produces neither a CR nor a heterosynaptic potentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and d.

claim: The mere potentiation of thalamic inputs is not sufficient to produce a memory, and some form of priming through associative or unpaired conditioning is essential.
source: As such, it appears that the mere potentiation of thalamic inputs is not sufficient to produce a memory, and some form of priming through associative or unpaired conditioning is essential.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The recovery of the conditioned response following the LTP protocol on the thalamic inputs (homoLTP) is unlikely to be a form of reinstatement.
source: Since we show that the thalamic inputs convey the footshock signal, the recovery of the CR following the LTP protocol on the same inputs (homoLTP) could be considered as a form of reinstatement, a well-known phenomenon where the mere presentation of a footshock after an extinguished CR reinstates the CR (Shirah et al., 2016; Bouton and Bolles, 1979). We think this is unlikely. First, we show that homoLTP is equally effective before the formation of the association. Additionally, we have shown previously that an LTP protocol is ineffective in restoring an extinguished CR (Nabavi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, supported by citations and previous work.

claim: Computational models simulating a circuit with comparable pre- and postsynaptic layouts yield similar results; that is heteroLTP stabilizes a weak memory.
source: It must be noted that computational models simulating a circuit with comparable pre- and postsynaptic layouts to ours yield similar results; that is heteroLTP stabilizes a weak memory.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to computational modeling work.

claim: According to computational models, heteroLTP in brain circuits with different pre- and postsynaptic arrangements may produce different physiological and behavioral outcomes.
source: However, according to these models, heteroLTP in brain circuits with different pre- and postsynaptic arrangements, may produce different physiological and behavioral outcomes (O'Donnell and Sejnowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to computational modeling work.

claim: Some forms of postsynaptic intracellular diffusion from strongly stimulated cortical inputs to weakly stimulated neighboring thalamic inputs could underlie the observed phenomena.
source: We consider some forms of postsynaptic intracellular diffusion from strongly stimulated cortical inputs to weakly stimulated neighboring thalamic inputs, as proposed by the Cross Talk and STC models.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism, referencing established models.

claim: Extracellular communication such as glutamate spillover is unlikely to underlie the observed phenomena.
source: On the other hand, we consider the possibility of extracellular communication (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1997) such as glutamate spillover to be unlikely. Extracellular communication is mainly reported in the circuits at early developmental stages which lack a tight extracellular matrix sheath (Asztely et al., 1997). Additionally, as we have shown here (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d) and reported by others (Doyère et al., 2003), LTP induction on the cortical input produces no heterosynaptic effect on the naïve thalamic inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, supported by citations and experimental evidence.

claim: The data point to an intracellular mechanism, which requires a prior priming but not necessarily a prior synaptic potentiation.
source: Taken together, our data point to an intracellular mechanism, which requires a prior priming but not necessarily a prior synaptic potentiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Exposure to a novel experience strengthens memory encoding in appetitive and aversive learning paradigms.
source: For example, it has been shown that exposure to a novel experience strengthens memory encoding in appetitive and aversive learning paradigms (Ballarini et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Activation of dopaminergic inputs to the hippocampus after memory encoding enhances memory persistence, mimicking the effect of environmental novelty.
source: Similarly, activation of dopaminergic inputs to the hippocampus after memory encoding enhances memory persistence, mimicking the effect of environmental novelty (Rossato et al., 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: De novo protein synthesis dependence and/or neuromodulator-signaling were suggested to be essential for the phenomenon of memory enhancement by novel experiences.
source: De novo protein synthesis dependence and/or neuromodulator-signaling were suggested to be essential for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a statement about established hypotheses in the field.

claim: Multiple pairings of optical co-activation of thalamic and auditory/associative cortical inputs with a footshock produce an enduring conditioned response.
source: We have previously shown that an enduring CR can be produced by multiple pairs of optical co-activation of thalamic and auditory/associative cortical inputs with a footshock (Nabavi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: An optical CS alone did not produce a conditioned response.
source: An optical CS alone did not produce a CR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Temporal (but not non-temporal) multiple pairings of the optical CS with a footshock produced a freezing response (CR) measured 24 hrs later.
source: whereas temporal (but not non-temporal) multiple pairings of the optical CS with a footshock produced a freezing response (CR) measured 24 hrs later (60%±7), indicating the formation of a long-term associative memory (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: HomoLTP was as effective in mice that were tested prior to the induction protocol as those that were not.
source: HomoLTP was as effective in mice that were tested prior to the induction protocol as those that were not (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: A homoLTP stimulus in naïve animals failed to produce a conditioned response.
source: It is notable that a homoLTP stimulus in naïve animals failed to produce a CR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A homoLTP stimulus produced a conditioned response as long as the animals received the conditioning protocol.
source: whereas it did produce a CR as long as the animals received the conditioning protocol (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: All opsins, regardless of their preferred excitation spectrum, are activated by blue light.
source: The main obstacle is that all opsins, regardless of their preferred excitation spectrum, are activated by blue light (Klapoetke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Recent attempts addressed the problem of independent optical activation by pairing blue-light sensitive anion channels with red-shifted ChR2.
source: Recent attempts addressed this problem by pairing blue-light sensitive anion channels with red-shifted ChR2, where red light derives action potentials, while blue light, through shunting inhibition, nullifies the effect of the red-shifted ChR2 (Mermet-Joret et al., 2021; Vierock et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The approach based on chloride influx is not suitable for axonal terminal activation, where the chloride concentration is high.
source: However, this approach, which is based on chloride influx, is not suitable for axonal terminal activation, where the chloride concentration is high (Mahn et al., 2018; Mahn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Yellow light minimally activates the blue-shifted ChR2, oChIEF.
source: It must be noted that yellow light minimally activates the blue-shifted ChR2, oChIEF, (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: The lateral thalamus collects signals from different brain regions of diverse modalities.
source: This can be explained by the fact that the lateral thalamus, the thalamic gateway to the LA, collects signals from different brain regions of diverse modalities (Barsy et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2022; Khalil et al., 2023; Ledoux et al., 1987; Linke et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The aversive signal to the lateral amygdala is conveyed largely through the thalamic inputs.
source: This further demonstrates that the aversive signal to the LA is conveyed largely through the thalamic inputs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Unpaired conditioning on the thalamic inputs does not produce synaptic potentiation.
source: It must be noted that previously we have shown that this protocol does not produce a detectable post-conditioning synaptic potentiation (Nabavi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: This observation is consistent with a previous report using only the unconditioned stimulus footshock.
source: This observation is consistent with a previous report using only the unconditioned stimulus footshock (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: This phenomenon is distinct from the paired form of conditioning which is receptive to homoLTP manipulation irrespective of the time of the delivery.
source: This phenomenon is distinct from the paired form of conditioning which is receptive to homoLTP manipulation irrespective of the time of the delivery (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the experimental data.

claim: Optical LTP protocols produce expected behavioral changes such as strengthening a memory.
source: We and others have shown that optical LTP protocols produce expected behavioral changes (Nabavi et al., 2014; Roy et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2017), such as strengthening a memory (Figures 1, 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figures 1, 3, and 4.

claim: All the mice with successful recall had successful potentiation of the synaptic input 24 hr after the induction of heteroLTP.
source: Our in vivo electrophysiology recordings from freely moving animals showed a strong correlation between synaptic potentiation and the successful recall of the aversive memory, as late as 24 hr after the induction of heteroLTP; all the mice with the successful recall had a successful potentiation of the synaptic input (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiology and behavioral data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: A lasting behavioral and electrophysiological consequence of heteroLTP has not been reported before.
source: Such a lasting behavioral and electrophysiological consequence of heteroLTP has not been reported before.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.
